gist: Labour is considering options to raise funds without increasing income tax, VAT or National Insurance.
Potential measures include higher bank surcharges, gambling taxes, online VAT enforcement and welfare cuts.
The government faces shrinking fiscal headroom alongside pressures from living costs and defence spending.

sections.heading: What happened
sections.text: The government faces a shrinking fiscal buffer, which economists estimate may have fallen from £24bn to £11bn. With manifesto pledges ruling out increases to income tax, VAT, or National Insurance, options to raise revenue include raising the corporation tax surcharge on banks and doubling the tax on electronic gaming machines. Another proposal would make online marketplaces such as Amazon, Ebay and Temu responsible for collecting VAT owed by platform sellers. Reducing welfare spending is also being considered.

sections.heading: Why it matters
sections.text: Chancellor John Healey needs funds to maintain fiscal rules, support defence spending and assist with the cost of living. The proposed tax measures could raise around £3.5bn annually, though critics highlight potential downsides. Gambling taxes could worsen odds for users, and online sellers might raise consumer prices. Restricting health and disability benefits could push recipients into poverty, while experts caution that required back-to-work support might offset immediate savings.

sections.heading: What happens next
sections.text: The Chancellor is expected to present the Budget on Wednesday. Any welfare reforms may face political hurdles, following previous backbench revolts over proposed benefit reductions.

gist: Gen Z users are fighting back against social media addiction and big tech platforms.
A growing digital detox industry offers apps and devices to limit screen time.
Young people are using DIY methods, alternative devices, and real-world networking apps instead.

sections.heading: What happened
sections.text: Gen Z users are pushing back against social media addiction. Many are turning to digital detox apps like Opal, alternative minimalist devices, or DIY tools to block distracting apps and limit screen time.

sections.heading: Why it matters
sections.text: Young people feel exploited and optimized for dopamine by tech platforms, leading to social isolation and regret. The digital detox market is growing rapidly as users seek to reclaim their lives.

sections.heading: What happens next
sections.text: The digital detox industry is projected to grow significantly by 2035, though convincing users to pay for subscriptions may prove challenging as many prefer free versions or simple deletions.

gist: Two British nationals have been charged following an investigation near RAF Fairford.
Police believe the alleged plot was intended to assist Iran's intelligence service.
The two charged men will appear at Westminster Magistrates' Court on Tuesday.

sections.heading: What happened
sections.text: Two British nationals, aged 24, have been charged following an investigation into a September incident near RAF Fairford. Outlets name one defendant as Mohmed Ahmad Abdulkarim of Westminster, while another names him Mohmed Abdulkarim of London. He is charged with assisting a foreign intelligence service, believed to be Iran's. The second man, Nouman Essghir, is charged with entering a prohibited place.

sections.heading: Why it matters
sections.text: Counter-terrorism police stated recent incidents have been directed by the Iranian state. RAF Fairford is used by the US Air Force, which flew bombers from there for defensive strikes against Iran before withdrawing them following threats. Iran has denied involvement.

sections.heading: What happens next
sections.text: The pair will appear at Westminster Magistrates' Court on Tuesday. Five other men remain on police bail.

timeline.text: Neil Young files second lawsuit against Trump for unauthorised use of Rockin’ in the Free World at rallies
Neil Young again sues Trump campaign for playing Rockin' in the Free World at rally

gist: Neil Young has sued a Donald Trump fundraising committee for ten million dollars.
The lawsuit alleges unauthorised use of Rockin' in the Free World at rallies.
Young previously sued Trump's campaign in 2020 over using the same song.

sections.heading: What happened
sections.text: Neil Young filed a ten-million-dollar copyright infringement lawsuit against Donald Trump's fundraising committee, the Trump 47 Committee. The rock musician alleges the campaign played his 1989 track Rockin' in the Free World without authorisation at a rally in Ohio on 12 October. Young previously sued Trump's re-election campaign in 2020 over the same song, which was settled.

sections.heading: Why it matters
sections.text: Young, an outspoken critic of Trump, argues the song contradicts Trump's platform and harms his reputation by falsely suggesting an endorsement. Under American copyright law, playing music at political events typically requires a public performance licence, which Young states he has never granted.

sections.heading: What happens next
sections.text: Young is seeking damages and an injunction to halt further public performances of the song. Trump's administration has not yet formally responded to the legal action.

A ten-million-dollar copyright infringement lawsuit was filed against a political committee.
The legal action follows a campaign rally held on 12 October.
The song was played at a campaign event in Youngstown, Ohio.
Young alleges his song was played publicly without permission or a licence.

sections.text: An Egyptian court convicted Mada Masr editor-in-chief Lina Attalah of managing an unlicensed website. The judge ordered the site's closure and a 3m Egyptian pounds fine. sections.heading: What happened
sections.text: An anonymous celebrity known as PPT asked the High Court to prevent ITN and Guardian News and Media from publishing allegations of inappropriate sexual activities. The man denies the claims. His legal team argued that publication would likely lead him to take his life, noting he had previously attempted suicide twice. The media organisations argued they have a duty to publish matters of public interest gathered from extensive investigations.

sections.heading: Why it matters
sections.text: The case involves a legal clash between protecting an individual's right to life and health against the freedom of expression and the public interest in publishing serious allegations. The judge must decide whether the story can be published, not whether the allegations are true.

sections.heading: What happens next
sections.text: The trial has concluded and Mr Justice Nicklin has retired to consider his ruling on whether the injunction will be granted.

sections.text: Three Florida brothers, Oren, Alon and Tal Alexander, were each sentenced in New York to 30 years in prison for sex trafficking. Several victims addressed the court during sentencing to describe the lasting psychological trauma caused by the attacks. The brothers denied the charges and maintained that the encounters were consensual.

sections.heading: Why it matters
sections.text: Prosecutors stated that the brothers exploited their luxury real estate business, financial influence and lavish lifestyle to target and dehumanise victims. Dozens of women came forward after initial allegations surfaced in 2024, with prosecutors alleging at least 70 women were assaulted.

sections.heading: What happens next
sections.text: US District Judge Valerie Caproni stated that the brothers should not serve their prison sentences in the same facility. However, defence lawyers argued that the men should be allowed to remain together.

sections.heading: What happened
sections.text: Artificial intelligence bots submitted tens of thousands of fake responses to a government consultation regarding the ban on disposable vapes in 2023. Authorities identified that seventy-six percent of the total submissions were machine-generated and opposed the proposed ban.

sections.text: Researchers note this is likely the first recorded instance of large-scale automated interference in UK public health policymaking. Such incidents threaten to distort public consultations and make corporate interests appear as popular public movements.

sections.text: John Healey delivered his first budget on Wednesday, tackling rising living costs against a turbulent global economic backdrop. sections.heading: Why it matters
sections.text: Stretched public finances and international market turmoil limited the chancellor's scope for big giveaways. The budget aimed to ease cost of living pressures responsibly while sticking to fiscal rules to reassure markets and protect public finances.

gist: Amy-Jane Beer gathered water from the Gypsey Race for a river rights charter.
Collaborators blended waters from across Yorkshire to create ink for the charter ceremony.
Participants swam at the confluence of the Ouse and Foss before the ceremony.

sections.heading: What happened
sections.text: Amy-Jane Beer visited the Gypsey Race stream in Yorkshire to request permission to collect water. She helped organise a gathering of river advocates co-drafting a regional charter of river rights. Water collected from various Yorkshire rivers, becks and springs was blended during a ceremony to make ink for writing the charter. Before the event, collaborators swam at the confluence of the Ouse and Foss.

sections.heading: Why it matters
sections.text: The Gypsey Race stream is associated with local folklore and prehistoric sites, including barrows, henges and England's tallest standing stone. Its flow is locally believed to hold the power of prophecy. The gathering aimed to make explicit people's responsibilities towards rivers through the charter.

gist: Political activist Tommy Robinson was found guilty of harassing two Daily Mail journalists.
He targeted reporters Andrew Young and Jacob Dirnhuber after the newspaper reported on his Cyprus holiday.
Robinson faces up to 10 years in prison and awaits sentencing on 16 December.

sections.heading: What happened
sections.text: Tommy Robinson was convicted of two counts of harassment causing fear of violence at Southwark Crown Court. He targeted journalists Andrew Young and Jacob Dirnhuber following a Daily Mail article about him in Cyprus. Robinson posted personal details online, hired private investigators, and made threatening calls.

sections.heading: Why it matters
sections.text: The prosecution stated that Robinson weaponised social media. The journalists and their families were forced to flee their homes and employ private security due to safety fears.

sections.heading: What happens next
sections.text: Robinson was granted bail and is scheduled to be sentenced on 16 December. He faces a maximum sentence of 10 years in prison.

fivew: Political activist Tommy Robinson, also known as Stephen Yaxley-Lennon.

He retaliated against reporters who published a story about him being in Cyprus during riots in England.

sections.heading: What happened
sections.text: Dolores Huerta, a pioneering civil rights activist and labour organiser, died in California on Wednesday aged 96. The BBC confirmed she died of cancer.

sections.heading: Why it matters
sections.text: Huerta co-founded the United Farm Workers union with Cesar Chavez, securing landmark contracts, overtime pay, and protections against heat deaths for agricultural labourers. She coined the rallying cry 'Sí, se puede!', helped negotiate immigration reforms, and championed women's and voting rights across several decades.

sections.heading: What happens next
sections.text: Huerta's family announced they will follow up on plans to recognise and celebrate her life and legacy.

Burnham warned ministers to remain disciplined regarding future UK relations with the EU.

sections.heading: What happened
sections.text: Prime Minister Andy Burnham ruled out calling a general election in the next 12 months. Opposition leaders Kemi Badenoch and Nigel Farage had claimed Burnham would hold an early vote. Burnham also told cabinet ministers not to express personal opinions on future EU relations.

sections.heading: Why it matters
sections.text: Opposition figures argued Burnham lacks a mandate after becoming prime minister following Sir Keir Starmer's resignation. Burnham countered that the Conservative Brexit deal caused low growth, but insisted government policy on EU relations must remain disciplined during this parliamentary term.

sections.heading: What happens next
sections.text: Burnham will attend a European summit next month to discuss initial Brexit changes within manifesto limits. Any major alterations to the UK's relationship with the EU will form part of a 10-year plan for the public to decide after the next election.

timeline.text: Tax thresholds remain unchanged - here's what it means for your pay

gist: Income tax thresholds will remain frozen until April 2031 as planned.
Frozen thresholds drag more people into paying tax and higher brackets.
A new Pension Tax Allowance will protect low-income pensioners from tax.

sections.heading: What happened
sections.text: Income tax thresholds remain frozen at current levels until April 2031. Although John Healey did not mention the end of this policy in his Budget speech, OBR documents show the freeze is scheduled to end after that date, after which thresholds are expected to rise again with inflation. The freeze has lowered take-home pay for the past five years.

sections.heading: Why it matters
sections.text: Freezing thresholds acts as a stealth tax, helping chancellors raise money for public services. By 2031, an extra 6.8 million people will pay tax and 5.4 million more will enter higher rate brackets. However, a new Pension Tax Allowance will ensure low-income pensioners do not pay income tax.

fivew: Income tax thresholds remain frozen until April 2031 before rising with inflation.
To raise extra money to help pay for public services like defence, the NHS and schools.

sections.heading: What happened
sections.text: Microsoft posted first-quarter fiscal 2027 revenue of $92.3 billion and net income of $33.6 billion. It simplified financial reporting into two segments: Agents and Infra, and Devices and Consumer. For the first time, Microsoft disclosed quarterly Azure dollar revenue, reporting $33.17 billion according to The Verge, or $33.2 billion according to TechCrunch. Meanwhile, Devices and Consumer revenue fell three percent, with Windows OEM and Xbox hardware sales declining.

sections.heading: Why it matters
sections.text: Disclosing Azure revenue allows direct comparisons with cloud competitors Alphabet and Amazon. Azure is now Microsoft's largest product line, exceeding analyst expectations with 48 percent growth. However, PC market contraction and Xbox restructuring continue to depress hardware and consumer performance.

sections.heading: What happens next
sections.text: Microsoft CFO Amy Hood expects Windows OEM and Xbox hardware declines to continue next quarter, though Xbox content and services revenue should rise. Microsoft is also proceeding with hybrid artificial intelligence rollouts across personal computers.

sections.heading: What happened
sections.text: A hacker known as the Department of Peace accessed DHS employee records through single sign-on service Okta. Working with cybersecurity researcher maia crimew, the data was published via Distributed Denial of Secrets under the name Icepick. The leak exposed details of over 41,000 personnel, mostly from CBP and ICE, alongside surveillance tools and covert operations. Okta stated it has no evidence its systems were compromised.

sections.heading: Why it matters
sections.text: The leak follows heightened scrutiny over immigration operations, which have caused fatal shootings. Immigration agents frequently conceal their identities during raids despite legal requirements to identify themselves. The publishers stated the breach intends to replace anonymity with accountability amid mass deportations, identifying key officials overseeing deportation and rendition programmes.

stories.standfirst: The construction of tourism facilities, housing, and infrastructure has surged in parts of Nepal and India's Uttarakhand.

articles.title: Building boom puts 300,000 people in the path of potential Himalayan disasters
articles.standfirst: The construction of tourism facilities, housing, and infrastructure has surged in parts of Nepal and India's Uttarakhand.

timeline.text: Building boom puts 300,000 people in the path of potential Himalayan disasters

gist: Built-up land in high-risk Himalayan zones grew by about 45% between 2016 and 2023.
At least 300,000 people now live in the path of potential Himalayan disasters.
Rapid warming speeds up glacier melting, destabilising slopes and expanding glacial lakes.

sections.heading: What happened
sections.text: A new study reveals that built-up land in high-risk zones across northern Nepal, Tibet, and India's Uttarakhand increased by roughly 45% between 2016 and 2023. Areas threatened by glacial lake flooding saw development rise by almost 78%. Tourism facilities, real estate, and infrastructure expanded rapidly along river banks and trekking regions.

sections.heading: Why it matters
sections.text: Warming in the Himalayas occurs at twice the global rate, accelerating glacier melt and destabilising mountain slopes. This increases the risk of catastrophic floods and landslides, threatening at least 300,000 people. Campaigners note that building regulations are poorly enforced and development has occurred without proper planning.

sections.heading: What happens next
sections.text: Authorities in Nepal plan to ban settlements within 15m of riverbanks along specific corridors, and Uttarakhand approved new floodplain zoning rules. However, experts warn that mitigating threats completely will remain a major challenge.

fivew: Researchers from the UK, Nepal, and India.
A study found significant development growth in high-risk Himalayan disaster zones.
Northern Nepal, south-eastern Tibet, and Uttarakhand in India.
Tourism, housing, and infrastructure expansion have outpaced safety planning amid regional warming.

sections.text: Russell Brand took the witness stand at Southwark Crown Court. He denied multiple charges of sexual offences involving six complainants across a decade. During questioning by his defence barrister, Brand stated that consent is essential and denied committing any of the alleged acts.

sections.heading: Why it matters
sections.text: The entertainer testified that publicity surrounding the claims affected his life and relationships deeply. He described losing support from peers and being barred from a hospital where his child underwent surgery.

gist: Chinese brands drop Kylian Mbappe after a joke about Mao Zedong.
Mbappe and La Liga have both issued formal apologies for the offence.
CCTV reportedly stopped showing La Liga matches following the online backlash.

sections.heading: What happened
sections.text: Kylian Mbappe laughed at a meme comparing him to a Chinese dictator during an interview. The clip circulated widely online, sparking an angry backlash in China over comments regarding Mao Zedong.

sections.heading: Why it matters
sections.text: Mao remains a sensitive and revered figure in China. The public backlash led major Chinese brands to terminate partnerships with Mbappe, and state media reportedly halted La Liga broadcasts.

sections.heading: What happens next
sections.text: Mbappe and La Liga have apologised, but Chinese brands continue to cut ties amid ongoing public opposition.

fivew: Chinese brands dropped Kylian Mbappe after he laughed at a meme referencing Mao Zedong.
After the comments circulated online following an interview.
Because his comments were deemed to have hurt the feelings of the Chinese people.

quotes.text: My comment was ill-judged, and I now understand that it hurt many people in China and in Chinese communities around the world
We have noted the relevant reports. Words and deeds that hurt the feelings of the Chinese people will naturally be met with opposition from all sectors of Chinese society.

timeline.text: Ballon d'Or in London - the most chaotic ever?

gist: The Ballon d'Or ceremony was held in London for the first time.
The event faced severe traffic delays, website blunders, and chaotic crowds.
Organisers apologised after a tense night featuring police clashes and protests.

sections.heading: What happened
sections.text: The Ballon d'Or ceremony at the London Palladium was delayed by 45 minutes due to heavy traffic and large crowds. Inside, the audience was rowdy and boisterous. Outside, barriers were broken, leading to clashes with police and two arrests. A website blunder also saw articles prematurely naming winners published online.

sections.heading: Why it matters
sections.text: The event was marked by major logistical issues, security breaches, and controversial moments during press conferences. The Ballon d'Or team has since issued an apology following complaints about female journalists being ignored during Harry Kane's press conference.

fivew: The Ballon d'Or ceremony experienced significant chaos including traffic delays, crowd disorder, and a website error.
Crowd behaviour, security breaches, and premature website publications caused widespread disruption.

sections.heading: What happened
sections.text: Thierry Henry hosted the Ballon d'Or ceremony alongside Kate Scott. He faced criticism for remarks made towards Lamine Yamal regarding his young player award, for correcting Scott's pronunciation of Socrates, and for admitting he wanted Kylian Mbappe to win the top prize over Harry Kane.

sections.heading: Why it matters
sections.text: Henry's comments drew an audible reaction from the audience and subsequent criticism on social media, leading him to release a video defending his actions and clarifying his intentions.

sections.heading: What happens next
sections.text: Henry has asked people to relax following the backlash over his hosting duties.

timeline.text: England out of tri-series after Sri Lanka beat Pakistan

gist: England were eliminated from the tri-series after Sri Lanka defeated Pakistan in Lahore.
Sri Lanka bowled Pakistan out for 110 and chased the target in 18.1 overs.
England will finish their tournament on Thursday before travelling to Australia for a tour.

sections.heading: What happened
sections.text: Sri Lanka defeated Pakistan by eight wickets in Lahore, eliminating England from the tri-series. Pakistan collapsed to 110 all out, with Dilshan Madushanka taking 5-34. Sri Lanka reached the target in 18.1 overs as Kamindu Mendis scored 62 not out.

sections.heading: Why it matters
sections.text: The exit interrupts England's recent momentum in one-day international cricket. After winning away in Sri Lanka and beating India and Sri Lanka at home in 2026, Harry Brook's side suffered three straight defeats in Pakistan.

sections.heading: What happens next
sections.text: England play Sri Lanka in a dead rubber on Thursday before travelling to Australia for a tour starting on 13 November. Sri Lanka will play Pakistan in Saturday's final.

timeline.text: 'I would do it again' - Kaepernick reflects on price of protest, 10 years on

gist: Colin Kaepernick reflects on kneeling during the US national anthem in 2016.
He believes his peaceful protest against racial injustice cost him his NFL career.
Kaepernick maintains he has no regrets and continues his activism a decade later.

sections.heading: What happened
sections.text: In September 2016, NFL quarterback Colin Kaepernick knelt during the US national anthem to protest racial injustice and police brutality. The action sparked widespread debate, inspiring other athletes while drawing criticism from political figures and leading to his exit from the NFL.

sections.heading: Why it matters
sections.text: The protest became a defining moment for modern athlete activism and civil rights, influencing global sports movements like taking the knee. Kaepernick argues that sports and politics are inherently linked and that current societal conditions demand more prominent protest.

sections.heading: What happens next
sections.text: Ten years on, Kaepernick has published a memoir titled The Perilous Fight and continues his philanthropic work and community campaigns while maintaining his fitness in case an opportunity to return to the NFL arises.

fivew: Colin Kaepernick reflected on his 2016 national anthem protests and the price he paid for athlete activism.
Ten years after his initial protest in September 2016.
To protest against racial injustice, police brutality, and the oppression of people of colour.

gist: Harry Kane won the Ballon d'Or at the London Palladium.
His career included challenging loan spells at Leyton Orient, Millwall, Norwich City, and Leicester City.
He achieved success at Tottenham Hotspur, Bayern Munich, and for England.

sections.heading: What happened
sections.text: Harry Kane won the Ballon d'Or at the London Palladium, beating Kylian Mbappe and Lamine Yamal. His career included loan spells at lower division clubs before breaking through at Tottenham Hotspur and later moving to Bayern Munich.

sections.heading: Why it matters
sections.text: He became the first English player to win the trophy since 2001 and the fifth overall, proving his doubters wrong through hard work and dedication.

sections.heading: What happens next
sections.text: After celebrations, Kane returns to business with Bayern Munich playing Magdeburg and Borussia Dortmund, while targeting potential success with England at Euro 2028.

fivew: Harry Kane won the Ballon d'Or.
His exemplary career and goalscoring success for club and country.

quotes.text: Work hard in silence. Let success be your noise.
